Oyster Bay

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A battle is brewing in a small coastal town in the Eastern Cape where a pristine beach meets a controversial mining plan.

Unique Selling Point:
Oyster Bay is a town of just 140 permanent residents. It's pristine beach and hiking trails are a drawcard for tourists. But, an application to mine a portion of the beach, has those living there, in an uproar. Many believe it will destroy the character of the coastal hamlet. Schoenmakers Mining, a holding company of Gqeberha-based Glendore Sand and Stone, plans to mine sand on a 5ha site on the primary dune - it will affect about half of the beach. The company applied for a permit in December last year, but residents say they have been left in the dark, and the public participation process has been non-existent. Residents claim they have been trying to register as interested and affected parties but that the mining company doesn't acknowledge their emails.

Summary:
According to the draft basic assessment report on the project compiled by Algoa Consulting Mining Engineers (Acme) on behalf of Schoenmakers Mining, the mine will operate for up to five years. There will also be an estimated 20 to 40 truckloads of sand being moved from the beach on a daily basis which will impact the only dirt road into and out of the town. The mining company believes the project will help the town overcome its sand migration problem, but residents don't buy this, and believe coastal sand mining will have a detrimental environmental impact. There are however some residents in favour of the mining company. These residents live in Brander street which is on the beachfront and sand encroachment has caused their homes to be "swallowed" by the dunes. They argue that the current so-called “mining” issue is a misnomer. What is proposed is not industrial-scale extraction, but rather controlled sand removal combined with ecological restoration. It’s a basic environmental management task, not resource exploitation. They say the intensity and irrationality of those in favour of the project resemble the behaviour of a cult.

Further information:
A 98 year old woman who bought her property in 1960 will talk to us about the changes over the years, the development of the town, its character and what makes it so special. A petition has been started as residents band together to fight the mining company. We speak to the Resident's Association, a tourist accommodation owner, and an environmental consultant about the possible consequences for this coastal town should the mining company get the go ahead.

Script:


VO 1 A remote coastal town in the Eastern Cape – fighting a losing battle against nature.

VO 2 Beachfront houses slowly swallowed by sand.

VO 3 Now, an application to mine the sand – to some the only means to save their properties – has split the town in two.

UPSOUND Una Bornman / Oyster Bay Resident: You can’t put a mine on the beach.
UPSOUND Keith Mutch / Oyster Bay property owner: The word mining for me is just horrendous. It’s just sand removal that’s all it is.
UPSOUND Walter Kurten / Oyster Bay Resident: Tourism is going to die in this town.

FADE TO BLACK

VO 4 Walter Kurten bought his home in Oyster Bay over twenty years ago, and moved here permanently when he retired.

VO 5 It was the bird life and the tranquility that attracted him.

VO 6 But, if a mining proposal goes ahead, that will change - for potentially up to five years.

UPSOUND Walter Kurten / Oyster Bay resident: It says there that between twenty and forty trucks is going to move through town every day, but they’ve made the exception that it won’t happen on weekends. I mean that’s stupid, that’s not a positive for us who lives here.

VO 7 A company called Schoenmakers Mining applied for a mining permit in December - that if granted, will mean the start of operations early next year.

UPSOUND Walter Kurten / Oyster Bay resident: We already have roads that not properly maintained. What do you think will happen to that roads in that five year period with forty trucks, or twenty or forty trucks on this little road?

VO 8 A roughly 20km road takes you into Oyster Bay. It’s a bumpy ride, as we discovered.

NATSOUND Sorry guys

VO 9 The journey is well worth it - a nature lover’s paradise.

LINK: It’s easy to see why many permanent residents of Oyster Bay are so protective of this place. For them, this is more than a mining application it’s a symbol of how small voices can be ignored in the world of big industry.

VO 10 Many feel the public participation process hasn’t been transparent. They’ve started a petition to stop the mining from going ahead, and will fight to protect their town.

UPSOUND Walter Kurten / Oyster Bay Residents Association: They want to make money. They won’t start a sand mine here if they not going to make a lot of money.

VO 11 And there’s no doubt there is plenty of money to be made. Sand is in high demand – even more than oil. It’s key for making concrete in the construction industry.

VO 12 It can range from industrial scale mining to relatively small operations, like the one planned at Oyster Bay. Here, a five hectare site has been demarcated for the operation – but, that’s nearly half of the 7km beach.

UPSOUND Rudi Gerber / Algoa Consulting Mining Engineers: Sand is becoming scarce worldwide. Forty billion tons of sand gets mined every year. Illegal mining of sand is a huge problem because it’s so easy to do. We’ve witnessed it.

VO 13 Rudi Gerber is a mining engineer who speaks on behalf of Schoenmakers Mining. His consulting company compiled the report for their application.

VO 14 Back in March, he reported sand being removed illegally from a sand covered street in the town, apparently for sale to local construction companies.

UPSOUND Rudi Gerber: It has many faces, its starts small with a person with a bakkie and a few shovels, it quickly goes over to a TLV and a truck. It could be big companies even in it.

VO 15 While illegal sand mining is hard to police, Gerber believes that if a mining permit is approved, it’ll benefit many in the area.

UPSOUND Rudi Gerber: New wind turbines are going to be constructed in the area and then the vast amounts of the sand are going into the foundations of these wind turbines. Obviously the mining company has to make a profit to pay for all the rehabilitation and everything for them to do it.

LINK: Clip 751 / Day 2 / Cam 1 For some battling with drifting dunes, sand mining is a possible solution, one they believe is being misrepresented. In a town this small, divisions cut deep, and what started as an environmental concern has become personal.

UPSOUND Keith Mutch / Oyster Bay property owner: This has absolutely split that community in half. Anything above the road, they’re against it, anything below the road, they’re all for it.

VO 16 Keith Mutch bought his beachfront property about twenty years ago. He lives in Cape Town, but dreamed of moving to Oyster Bay permanently.

ERIN: Keith, how much has all of this headache cost you?
UPSOUND Keith Mutch: So, over the course of the last fifteen years its probably cost me the thick end of a million. In fact, what happens now is my wife sends me a week before she comes and I go there to dig sand.

VO 17 And they’re not the only ones. This house has become completely inaccessible.

UPSOUND Gill Brandstetter / Oyster Bay property owner: We have to always climb dunes to get to our property.

VO 18 Gill Brandstetter and her family bought their holiday home back in 2012. And over the years they’ve made many memories here.

ERIN: At the time did you know that the dunes were going to be a potential hazard?
UPSOUND Gill Brandstetter: Well, we were kind of spontaneous about buying there because it was right on the beach and beautiful, but I think only later did we realise hang on, you know, this could be a problem.

VO 19 Their plans to retire here have been put on hold.

UPSOUND Gill Brandstetter:Ten years ago it was okay, it was easier, but we are senior citizens so clambering over dunes you know, it’s still doable, but it’s blimming hard.

VO 20 The removal of the sand will, they believe, solve their problems.

UPSOUND Gill Brandstetter: The mining company says they going to slope it down as it was in the past. So, it’s going to be beautified.
UPSOUND Keith Mutch: There seems to have been an issue that we’ve got a mining company that’s moving in, and they going to set up mining houses, and big graders and twenty four hour a day trucks running around, so kids can’t play on the beach. And, it’s just nonsense.

VO 21 The Kouga Local Municipality redistributes sand along the beach once or twice a year. But, actually removing it, requires a mining permit.

VO 22 Schoenmakers Mining, in its application, promises a number of benefits - including job creation.

UPSOUND Walter Kurten: They going to bring their technical people in from outside. The people that’s going to get jobs are going to be flag wavers.

UPSOUND Rudi Gerber: A small scale mine like this will create four or five employment opportunities.
ERIN Four or five?
UPSOUND Rudi Gerber: Very small, but for every person directly employed in the mining industry in South Africa, more or less 38 downstream employment is also created.

VO 23 Astonishingly, the Kouga Local Municipality confirmed in a whatsapp response that it only became aware of the mining application during the public participation process, saying that while there would be certain benefits, damage to municipal infrastructure remains a concern.

ON SCREEN: While sand mining in the Oyster Bay area will have certain benefits, the actual operations and control over the mining process and possible damage to municipal infrastructure remains a concern.

VO 24 Gerber says the public participation period is still open and he’s happy to have one on one meetings with concerned residents.

UPSOUND Rudi Gerber: The biggest benefactors of it all will be the Municipality. Their land value will be enhanced. The residents, their land values will be enhanced as well because the sand will not blow up onto them anymore.

VO 25 Not only that. Schoenmakers confidently says the problem will be solved for up to fifty years. A claim dismissed by environmental consultant, Dr Werner Illenberger.

UPSOUND Dr Werner Illenberger / Environmental Consultant: The sand will have to be removed all the time. It’s a continuous management problem that resulted from building the houses where they shouldn’t really be.

VO 26 Dr Illenberger specialises in coastal dunes and says sand encroachment is a result of natural processes.

UPSOUND Dr Werner Illenberger: The dunes used to blow for thousands of years right across this peninsula ending up in St Francis bay actually. But, where people had built houses and extended the township, it caused big problems for the people living there.

VO 27 He believes sand mining is a good solution.

UPSOUND Dr Werner Illenberger: The environmental impact is negligible.

VO 28 That’s not a view shared by Oyster Bay’s oldest resident, who says mining will change the character of the town. At 98, Una Bornman still vividly remembers the holidays spent here with her family.

VO 29 They bought property here in 1960 and Una moved here permanently over fifty years ago. Her son Nick eventually followed.


ERIN: So you’ve seen a lot of changes over the years?
UPSOUND Una Bornman / Oyster Bay Resident:I’ve seen a lot of changes but the wind doesn’t change. The wind blows and blows and blows in the winter.

VO 30 Sand migration has been happening for centuries, and Nick, who runs the Oyster Bay Beach Lodge, says it’s been a problem for residents for decades.

UPSOUND Nick Bornman: Personally I feel sorry for the people that’s got problems with the sand in their homes. But, on the other side, they bought properties right behind a sand dune knowing they will have that problem eventually.

VO 31 For Una, Mother Nature will triumph in the end anyway. For her, the sound of the wind is a reminder that no matter what we build ….the dunes will always return.

UPSOUND Una Bornman / Oyster Bay resident: You can’t change the wind. The wind will continue blowing from the west to the east. They should never have built here. Never have built here.

Her son Nick eventually followed. ERIN: So you’ve seen a lot of changes over the years? UPSOUND Una Bornman / Oyster Bay Resident:I’ve seen a lot of changes but the wind doesn’t change. The wind blows and blows and blows in the winter. VO 30 Sand migration has been happening for centuries, and Nick, who runs the Oyster Bay Beach Lodge, says it’s been a problem for residents for decades. UPSOUND Nick Bornman: Personally I feel sorry for the people that’s got problems with the sand in their homes. But, on the other side, they bought properties right behind a sand dune knowing they will have that problem eventually. VO 31 For Una, Mother Nature will triumph in the end anyway. For her, the sound of the wind is a reminder that no matter what we build ….the dunes will always return. UPSOUND Una Bornman / Oyster Bay resident: You can’t change the wind. The wind will continue blowing from the west to the east. They should never have built here. Never have built here.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A battle is brewing in a small coastal town in the Eastern Cape where a pristine beach meets a controversial mining plan.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Oyster Bay is a town of just 140 permanent residents. It's pristine beach and hiking trails are a drawcard for tourists. But, an application to mine a portion of the beach, has those living there, in an uproar. Many believe it will destroy the character of the coastal hamlet. Schoenmakers Mining, a holding company of Gqeberha-based Glendore Sand and Stone, plans to mine sand on a 5ha site on the primary dune - it will affect about half of the beach. The company applied for a permit in December last year, but residents say they have been left in the dark, and the public participation process has been non-existent. Residents claim they have been trying to register as interested and affected parties but that the mining company doesn't acknowledge their emails.
metadata.Summary: According to the draft basic assessment report on the project compiled by Algoa Consulting Mining Engineers (Acme) on behalf of Schoenmakers Mining, the mine will operate for up to five years. There will also be an estimated 20 to 40 truckloads of sand being moved from the beach on a daily basis which will impact the only dirt road into and out of the town. The mining company believes the project will help the town overcome its sand migration problem, but residents don't buy this, and believe coastal sand mining will have a detrimental environmental impact. There are however some residents in favour of the mining company. These residents live in Brander street which is on the beachfront and sand encroachment has caused their homes to be "swallowed" by the dunes. They argue that the current so-called “mining” issue is a misnomer. What is proposed is not industrial-scale extraction, but rather controlled sand removal combined with ecological restoration. It’s a basic environmental management task, not resource exploitation. They say the intensity and irrationality of those in favour of the project resemble the behaviour of a cult.
metadata.Further information: A 98 year old woman who bought her property in 1960 will talk to us about the changes over the years, the development of the town, its character and what makes it so special. A petition has been started as residents band together to fight the mining company. We speak to the Resident's Association, a tourist accommodation owner, and an environmental consultant about the possible consequences for this coastal town should the mining company get the go ahead.
